finalShorts.title: How Did Medieval Londoners Go to the Toilet?
finalShorts.description:
How did people go to the toilet in medieval London? Public latrines, household cesspits and the night work of gong farmers reveal a less glamorous side of city life in 1390.

Watch the full episode on our channel: What Did People in Medieval London Actually Do All Day?

Sources: Ernest L. Sabine, Latrines and Cesspools of Mediaeval London (1934); Calendar of Coroners Rolls of the City of London, 1300–1378 (1913).

Illustrated history by Life, Previously.

finalShorts.title: Did Medieval People Really Drink Beer Instead of Water?
finalShorts.description:

Sources: Caroline M. Barron, London in the Later Middle Ages (2004); Judith M. Bennett, Ale, Beer, and Brewsters in England (1996).

finalShorts.title: 7 Years, No Wife: Life as a Medieval Apprentice
finalShorts.description:
An apprenticeship in medieval London meant at least seven years learning a trade—and no marriage until the term was done. Your master provided food, housing and training. In return, you worked and obeyed.

Watch the full episode on our channel: What Did People in Medieval London Actually Do All Day?

Source: Barbara A. Hanawalt, Growing Up in Medieval London (1993).

finalShorts.title: Where Did People in Pompeii Go to the Toilet?
finalShorts.description:
In many Pompeii houses the toilet sat right in the kitchen. And in one alley, a painted warning: "Crapper, beware of trouble."

Watch the full episode on our channel: What Was Written on Pompeii's Walls Before the Eruption?

Sources: A. O. Koloski-Ostrow, The Archaeology of Sanitation in Roman Italy (2015); Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum IV 7714–7716.

Illustrated history by Life, Previously.

finalShorts.title: What Did a Drink Cost in Pompeii?
finalShorts.description:
A bar wall in Pompeii still carries a price list: "Hedone says: you can drink here for one copper. Pay two, and you'll drink better." What did a drink cost before Vesuvius erupted in AD 79?

Watch the full episode on our channel: What Was Written on Pompeii's Walls Before the Eruption?

Source: Hedone's price list, Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum IV 1679.

Illustrated history by Life, Previously.

finalShorts.title: Pompeii's Gladiators Had Fans. Then Came the Riot.
finalShorts.description:
"Celadus the Thracian, the girls' heartthrob", scratched in the gladiators' barracks. Twenty years before the eruption, a show in Pompeii's amphitheatre ended in a riot.

Watch the full episode on our channel: What Was Written on Pompeii's Walls Before the Eruption?

Sources: Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum IV 4342; Tacitus, Annals 14.17.

publicDescriptionChecks.title: What Did People in Medieval London Actually Do All Day?
publicDescriptionChecks.description:
What was daily life in medieval London really like? Spend one ordinary day in London in 1390 and see how working people lived in the Middle Ages, from the church bells before dawn to the curfew bell at night.

You wake up beside three strangers, sign on as an apprentice for at least seven years with no marrying until it's done, find out what medieval people ate and drank, queue at a cookshop for a hot pie, meet the gong farmers who emptied the city's cesspits, and see what Londoners did for fun before the city gates shut.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Cold open
1:00 Woken by bells
2:20 Breakfast and the beer-or-water myth
3:25 Work: apprentices, sunrise to sunset
4:58 Dinner: takeaway pies from a cookshop
5:56 The streets: toilets, cesspits and gong farmers
7:06 Free time: football, archery and the alehouse
8:12 The last bell: curfew and the Tun

Also in this video: whether medieval people really drank beer because the water would kill them (only half true), the Great Conduit that piped spring water into the city, why London's spur makers had to stop work at the curfew bell in 1345, why a legal wage cap failed after the Black Death, the public toilet on London Bridge, Richard the Raker's fatal fall into his cesspit in 1326, the 1314 football ban, Edward III's archery order, and the Tun on Cornhill, where nightwalkers were locked up.

SOURCES
Caroline M. Barron, London in the Later Middle Ages (2004)
Barbara A. Hanawalt, Growing Up in Medieval London (1993)
H. T. Riley (ed.), Memorials of London and London Life (1868)
Martha Carlin, "Fast Food and Urban Living Standards in Medieval England" (1998)
C. M. Woolgar, The Culture of Food in England, 1200-1500 (2016)
Judith M. Bennett, Ale, Beer, and Brewsters in England (1996)
Ernest L. Sabine, "Latrines and Cesspools of Mediaeval London" (1934) and "City Cleaning in Mediaeval London" (1937)
R. R. Sharpe (ed.), Calendar of Coroners Rolls of the City of London, 1300-1378 (1913)
John Stow, A Survey of London (1598)
Ian Mortimer, The Time Traveller's Guide to Medieval England (2008)
Liber Albus: The White Book of the City of London (1419), trans. H. T. Riley (1861)
R. R. Sharpe (ed.), Calendar of Letter-Books of the City of London (1899-1912)
H. M. Chew and W. Kellaway (eds), London Assize of Nuisance 1301-1431 (1973)
Dolly Jørgensen, "Modernity and Medieval Muck", Nature and Culture 9.3 (2014)
Ruth Mazo Karras, Common Women: Prostitution and Sexuality in Medieval England (1996)
John Schofield, Medieval London Houses (1994)

On-screen documents: Great Conduit (begun 1245); Articles of the Spurriers (1345); Statute of Labourers (1351); London cooks' price list (1378); city street-cleaning order (1357); coroner's roll (1326); mayor's proclamation against football (1314, Liber Memorandorum fol. 66); order of Edward III (1363); Statutes of the City of London (1285); the Tun on Cornhill (built 1282, per Stow).
Every claim in this video was checked against its source; the full claim sheet with page references is available on request.

Music: "Life, Previously" theme, made for this channel.

publicDescriptionChecks.title: What Was Written on Pompeii's Walls Before the Eruption?
publicDescriptionChecks.description:
What did ordinary people in Pompeii write on their walls before Vesuvius erupted in AD 79?

Spend a day in Pompeii through its residents' own words: rent notices, election posters painted by lamplight, a bar's wine prices, insults, love notes, toilet warnings and gladiator fan mail. Then find out what really happened when the eruption came, and why most people probably got out.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Cold open
1:10 Water on every corner
2:16 A room to let
3:15 Breakfast at the counter
5:06 Wool, work and urine
6:09 Election season
7:35 Baths, toilets and gossip
9:15 The games
10:26 The end of the story

SOURCES
Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum IV (the Pompeii inscriptions), via the Epigraphik-Datenbank Clauss-Slaby and the Ancient Graffiti Project
Parco Archeologico di Pompei, excavation reports and E-Journal degli Scavi di Pompei (2018-2026)
G. Zuchtriegel et al., "La data della distruzione di Pompei" (2024)
Pliny the Younger, Letters 6.16 and 6.20; Tacitus, Annals 14.17 and 15.22; Seneca, Natural Questions 6
E.-M. Viitanen, "Painting Signs in Ancient Pompeii" (2020)
K. Korhonen, E.-M. Viitanen, L. Nissin, "Inscriptions in their spatial contexts in Roman Italy" (2015)
L. Savunen, "Women and elections in Pompeii" (1995)
A. Kolb (ed.), Literacy in Ancient Everyday Life (2018)
M. Flohr and A. Wilson (eds), The Economy of Pompeii (2017)
R. Olsson, The water-supply system in Roman Pompeii (2015); M. Notarian, "Water Distribution from Public Fountains in Pompeii" (2023)
A. O. Koloski-Ostrow, The Archaeology of Sanitation in Roman Italy (2015)
G. Luongo et al., "Impact of the AD 79 explosive eruption on Pompeii" (2003); P. Dellino et al., Scientific Reports (2021)
E. Pilli et al., "Ancient DNA challenges prevailing interpretations of the Pompeii plaster casts", Current Biology (2024)

On-screen documents: Hedone's price list (CIL IV 1679); Julia Felix's rental notice (CIL IV 1136); election notices (CIL IV 7621, 3884); "I marvel, wall" (CIL IV 1904); the Regio V food counter (2019-2020); the Regio IX mill-room (2023); children's charcoal drawings (published 2024); Celadus (CIL IV 4342); "Crapper, beware" (CIL IV 7714-7716); the amphitheatre riot painting (after AD 59); a household spending list (CIL IV 5380); the charcoal date note (found 2018); Scaurus' fish-sauce mosaic.
Every claim in this video was checked against its source; the full claim sheet is available on request.

Music: "Life, Previously" theme, made for this channel.
